newsitem.title: UK: Swissie recaptures haven status amid EMU worries.
newsitem.headline: Swissie recaptures haven status amid EMU worries.

text.p: The Swiss franc, which had been sidelined on the foreign exchanges in recent months, has suddenly found itself in the spotlight again by recapturing its former status as a safe-haven European currency.

The Swiss franc's paltry interest rate yield, the lowest in Europe, had overshadowed its traditional haven status over the past year. The franc weakened sharply as investors aggressively borrowed cheap francs to sell for higher-yielding units.

In recent weeks, however, there's been a growing perception of a Europe-friendly government in Britain and the possibility of a new French government that will opt for broad-based membership of European monetary union, analysts say.
This is making punters worried about betting on currencies linked to the euro, which would likely become weaker in direct proportion to the number of members.
"The Swiss franc is being seen as perhaps one of the few major currencies not involved in the single European currency," said Robert Hayward, economic advisor at Bank America here.

The Swiss franc hit a five-month high of 84.37 centimes per mark on Friday after ending European trade at 84.50/52 on Thursday. It trod a similar, albeit less marked, path against the dollar, rising to a one-month high of 1.4331 per dollar against its previous close here of 1.4406/16.
"Over the past few days there's been a bit of worry over EMU and the French elections, so the Swiss franc is being used as a sort of haven," said Peter Wood, dealer at Bank of Boston here.

"There's a lot of movement away from sterling, with a lot of positions built up against the Swiss franc and mark and yen over the past several months, and they're all panicking out at the present time," Wood said.

Sterling suffered a body blow on Thursday after a wire report quoted a source in Britain's new ruling Labour Party as saying the pound should go back into the European exchange rate mechanism in 2001 at a rate of 2.50 marks.
The UK Treasury was quick to rubbish the report, but talk about it lingered on. A shaky pound was down nearly seven pfennigs from Tuesday's peak on Friday.

Since the Maastricht treaty on EMU stipulates a currency must be in the ERM for at least two years to qualify as an EMU member, Thursday's report fuelled speculation the UK Labour party, which came to power last week for the first time in 18 years, was beginning to lean towards joining monetary union.
Meanwhile, EMU worries have been stoked by opinion polls indicating an increasing possibility the left-wing could triumph in France's National Assembly elections on May 25 and June 1.
The French Socialists have set certain conditions for joining the euro, including the entry of Italy and Spain and that the euro should not be overvalued.
A poll by Ipsos on Thursday showed the current ruling coalition with its narrowest lead yet, with a forecast of 290 seats against a combined 286 for the Socialists and Communists.

"The Socialists have made it clear that they want EMU to go ahead...but they have no intention of letting it go ahead entirely on German conditions," said Elizabeth Legge, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London.

"So it's surprising that the franc hasn't come off already, but perhaps there's a feeling that we still have to wait until the actual elections," she said, adding that there had been evidence for some time that the Socialists were gaining.
The French franc was trading at 3.3741/46 per mark against 3.3732/35 late on Thursday.
Analysts say all this bodes well for the Swiss franc, but some say its rally may not last for long.
"It's likely to dry up, I would think that the Swiss National Bank would want the rally to stop," Bank America's Hayward said.
"The current strength in the Swiss franc may encourage them to try and do something about it...by putting liquidity into the money market to push short-term interest rates down."
